Coccidioidomycosis is a fungal disease endemic to the deserts of the American southwest, parts of Mexico, and Cenral and South America. Most infections present 1-3 weeks after exposure as community acquired pneumonia, but nonmeningeal dissemination and meningitis can also result.

21,037 cases in 2023, mostly in California and Arizona, USA. This number is likely significantly higher, but with self limited disease and low test rates, disease is under-recognized. Based on a cross-sectional study from 2019, it is estimated that the number of cases is 10-18 times the number reported by national surveillence.

In 2017, the number of cases rose significantly, predominantly in California and Arizona, USA. The cause of the rise of cases is multifactorial and debated: increased travel to endemic areas, climatic and envronmental changes, and improvement in awareness, surveillance, testing, and diagnosis.In a US study using the Pediatric Health Information System (PHIS), a national inpatient database, hospital incidence rates increased significantly between 2003-2005 and 2005-2006 (8.31/100,000 discharges vs 12.95/100,000 discharges).
As of 2017, coccidomycosis had been identified in 22 states in the US.
95% of cases occur in southern California and Arizona.
It is the cause of 15-30 percent of community-aquired pneumonias in the Phoenix and Tucson metropolitan areas.
It is caused by fungal species Coccidioides immitis and Coccidioides posadasii found in soil in endemic areas.
Coccidioidomycosis is transmitted by inhalation of dispersed, contaminated soil.
After being ingested, it can spread hematogenously to bone, meninges, and skin.
See for the risk factors for severe or disseminated disease.
If a patient who resides in or who has traveled to the endemic area presents with symptoms of pneumonia, consider laboratory evaluation for coccidioidomycosis. C
In patients with symptomatic disease, coccidioides enzyme immunoassay is a rapid, dependable diagnostic tool. C

If disseminated disease is suspected, histologic examination and culture of suspicious skin lesions, analysis of joint effusion aspirates and lumbar punctures for patients with meningeal signs should be utilized as appropriate. C
See for the Differential Diagnosis
Approximately 60% of patient are asymptomatic or have mild disease.
Of patients who are symptomatic, approximately 60% present with isolated pulmonary disease. 5-10% of patients have complicated disease and dissemination is rare.
Cough is the most common symptom (80%), followed by fever (45%) and dyspnea (26%).Onset of symptoms typically occurs 1-3 weeks after exposure
Patients also often expereince weight loss, night sweats, fatigue and headache.

Immunologic and rheumatologic symptoms are common. The most common immunologic finding is erythema nodosa, followed by erythema multiforme or generalized rash. The most common rheumatologic manifestation is arthralgias, which can be severe.
In a 12-year retrospective study of 71 patients with coccidioidomycosis involving the CNS, headache was the only symptom found in the majority of patients.
Dissemination can occur to the skin, bone, joints, meninges, and other soft tissues and results in a variety of different physical findings.
Laboratory evaluation for coccidioidomycosis should be strongly considered for patients who reside in or have traveled to endemic areas and present with CAP symptoms for more than 1 week in duration.

In patients with symptomatic disease, coccidioides enzyme immunoassay is a rapid, dependable diagnostic tool. Positive results should have confirmatory testing with immunodiffusion or complement fixation to rule out false positives and provide diagnostic confirmation.
PCR is another available diagnostic tool that has greater sensitivity and specificity but is not as widely available.
A white blood cell count with differential can be helpful as 25% of patients will have eosinophilia of more than 5%.
Common chest x-ray findings include a unilateral dense infiltrate, hilar or mediastinal adenopathy, and occasionally nodular cavitary lesions (4-8%).
In patients with headaches or neurologic symptoms, brain imaging with MRI as well as a lumbar puncture should be performed to rule out coccidioidal meningitis.

In a retrospective case series of patients with CNS involvement, CSF anticoccidioidal antibody and culture were frequently negative on presentation, but the serum antibody test was usually positive. Imaging studies were helpful in two thirds of cases (most often demonstrating basilar meningitis or hydrocephalus).
Complement fixation titers of 1:32 or greater are associated with complicated infections including dissemination to bone or skin and chronic disease.
Culture, though definitive, is not often utilized because it can take 7 to 10 days, there is a significant risk of transmission to laboratory personnel, and is not reliable for CSF.
Histopathology of infected tissue will show the double-walled spherule with endospores.

Coccidioidomycosis should be suspected in patients who have been exposed to endemic areas and who present with fever, cough, dyspnea, and pulmonary infiltrates. Suspicion should be especially high for patients who have occupations which expose them to soil such as farmers, archaeologists, military personnel, and construction workers and for those who are immunocompromised.
Confirmatory tests include enzyme immunoassay with immunodiffusion/complerment fixation, PCR, histopathology, and culture.

Empiric therapy is generally not necessary as most primary infections resolve without treatment. For immunocompromised and other patients who would warrant treatment, oral azole therapy should be initiated. Amphotericin B is reserved for disemminated or refractory disease, or in first trimester of pregnancy. (see ).
Immunocompetent patients with acute uncomplicated coccidioidal pneumonia who do not have other risk factors for dissemination or severe disease do not require antifungal therapy. C
Conditions that warrant treatment of acute uncomplicated coccidioidal pneumonia are immunosuppression, preexisting cardiopulmonary disease, and third trimester pregnancy. C
Persistent or progressive pneumonia as well as disseminated disease should be treated with oral fluconazole 400 mg/day or itraconazole 200 mg twice daily. A
Oral fluconazole 400 mg/day is effective treatment for coccidioidal meningitis and the treatment should be lifelong. A
Amphotericin B is the treatment of choice for pregnant patients in first trimester and is an alternative for patients with miliary and progressive disseminated disease.C

Most primary infections resolve without treatment. If the patient is immunocompetent and does not have other risk factors for dissemination or severe disease, reassessment of symptoms and radiographic findings every 1-3 months for 1 year is appropriate. Overuse of azoles such as fluconazole increase the likelihood of resistance, which is increasing.

Conditions that warrant treatment of acute uncomplicated coccidioidal pneumonia are immunosuppression, preexisting cardiopulmonary disease, and third trimester pregnancy. Due to their associated risk of dissemination, patients of African American or Filipino descent should also be considered for treatment. The treatment for uncomplicated acute coccidioidal pneumonia is an oral azole for 3-6 months, except for pregnant patients, in which case Amphotericin B is the treatment of choice.

In an RCT of 198 patients with chronic coccidioidal infections, oral fluconazole (400 mg/d) was equivalent in overall efficacy to itraconazole (200 mg/d) in nonmeningeal coccidiodomycosis; however, itraconazole was more effective in skeletal infections. Posaconazole 400 mg/day shows promise as another treatment for coccidiomycosis.

Treatment should be initiated for persistent or progressive pneumonia and should be continued for at least 1 year. Amphotericin B can be used as an initial treatment if the patient is hypoxic or rapidly deteriorating. Amphotericin B should be discontinued and replaced with an oral azole after the patient's condition improves - usually within several weeks.

Disseminated disease should also be treated with an oral azole. In general, amphotericin B should be reserved for patients who do not respond to treatment with oral azoles or who have lesions in vital locations such as the vertebral column.

The ideal treatment duration for nonmeningeal disseminated disease is unclear. Treatment courses range from months to years. Regardless of when treatment is discontinued, follow up should be conducted every several months for several years due to the risk of relapse.

Coccidiodal meningitis: Oral fluconazole 400 mg/day is effective suppressive therapy for coccidioidal meningitis. Oral azole therapy for coccidioidal meningitis should be lifelong due to the significant relapse rate after discontinuation of treatment.
Common side effects of fluconazole include dermatologic reactions, QTc prolongation, and hepatotoxicity. Treatment with amphotericin B requires monitoring of renal function and electrolytes.

Asymptomatic pulmonary nodules and cavities do not require surgical excision and periodic radiographs for 2 years to assess stability is appropriate. If the cavity persists for the 2 years, resection may be considered.

Treatment for symptomatic pulmonary cavities includes surgical resection in conjunction with oral azoles. Similarly, treatment for ruptured cavities includes lobectomy with decortication in addition to antifungal therapy.
Large abscesses, pneumothorax, instability of the spine, and impingement of vital organs may also necessitate surgical intervention.
Persistent or progressive pneumonia, nonmeningeal dissemination and CNS involvement may necessitate hospitalization at least until the patient has stabilized.
Immunocompromise and pregnancy may also necessitate hospitalization.
Most primary infections resolve without treatment. B
Mortality in hospitalized patients was 5 % in children and 7% in adults, as was the need for surgical intervention (41%). In-hospital mortality was low (1.5%). B
Most primary infections resolve without treatment.
The disease can progress to diffuse pulmonary disease, pulmonary nodules or cavities, or chronic pulmonary disease and can disseminate to skin, joints, and meninges.
in 2023 there were 500 coccidioidomycosis-associated deaths in the US.
Among hospitalized patients the mortality rates were 5% in children and 7% in adults.
There is a 71% relapse rate for CNS disease.
Nonwhite race, especially Filipino and African American, is a predictor for dissemination.
Regardless of when treatment is discontinued, follow up should be conducted every several months for several years due to the risk of relapse.
Older patients are considered at higher risk for severe infection and initiating anti fungal treatment should be strongly considered.

Treatment should be initiated for pregnant patients, especially those in the third trimester, however if a patient is clinically stable without treatment, consider no medication furing first trimester and azole during the second and third.

Amphotericin B is the treatment of choice for pregnant patients in the first trimester and is an alternative treatment for patients with aggressive miliary or disseminated disease with dosing of 0.5 to 1.0 mg/kg. In the second and third trimester of pregnancy, transition to azole can be considered.
Fluconazole is avoided in first trimester because of teratogenicity.
For patients with HIV, prophylaxis is not recommended.
Treatment is recommended in HIV patients if the patient has clinically active coccidioidomycosis and a CD4 count <250. Treatment may be discontinued if the CD4 count increases to >250.
In other immunocompromised patients, treat with azoles.

cell.label: Suspected coccidioidomycosis: pneumonia symptoms in patient exposed to endemic areas. Order serology. Result?
If the patient is pregnant, treat with amphotericin B in the first trimester and azoles in the second and third. Immunocompetent?

No antifungal therapy required. Conduct reassessment at 1-month to 3-month intervals for at least 1 year. Begin treatment with oral azole if pulmonary disease progresses or disseminates, or if symptoms persist for more than 2 months.
Signs of dissemination to meninges or other soft tissue?
Histologic examination and culture of suspicious skin lesions, analysis of joint effusion aspirates or lumbar puncture. Result?
Treat with oral azole. Amphotericin B for patients who do not respond to treatment with oral azoles or who have lesions in vital locations.
Treat with oral azole for 3-6 months.
